conversations.notes: Quick coffee at the conference. Marcus said the strategy team is six people and works closely with the CEO. He thinks summer interns get one real project, usually a market-entry analysis for a new state. He suggested I apply early because they close the application in November.

Twenty-minute call. Elena explained that base-village projects take seven to ten years from land purchase to opening. Most of her team are real-estate people, not ski people. She was not sure whether Granite Peak takes summer MBA interns and said she would ask HR.

sample_notes.priya: Call with Priya Raman, 30 minutes. She said the biggest difference between development and asset management is timing: developers own a project from site selection through financing, while asset managers take over once it is operating. Her developers spend maybe 30 percent of their time on models and the rest negotiating land leases, interconnection and offtake contracts. She said most of Cascade's developers live in Denver or Boulder, but two work remotely from Durango. Cascade usually hires two MBA interns and decides by mid-January. She offered to introduce me to Luis Ortega, who runs their storage team. I should send her my resume this week and read up on the interconnection queue before we talk again.
sample_notes.sam: Phone call with Sam Okafor. Sam said Basecamp has eleven people and every project manager spends two or three days a week on site during the building season. Most of their money comes from towns and counties using public grants, so projects depend on grant timing. He said pay is lower than energy but there is profit sharing. He would consider a summer MBA fellow if the person could own grant applications for two projects. He asked me to send a one-page note on how I would approach the grant pipeline by November 10.
